units.t: How Habits Actually Form.
Part one. Life on autopilot.
Think back to this morning.
Which side of the bed did you get out of?
Which shoe did you put on first?
What did you do with your hands while the kettle boiled?
Chances are you can't quite remember, and that's not because your memory is bad.
It's because you weren't really deciding any of it.
You were running on habit.
In the late 1890s, the American psychologist William James wrote that all our life, so far as it has definite form, is but a mass of habits.
More than a century later, researchers set out to measure how true that was.
In a diary study published in 2002, the psychologist Wendy Wood and her colleagues asked university students to note down what they were doing, thinking and feeling.
They made an entry once an hour, through the day.
About forty-three per cent of their actions were things they did almost every day, in the same place, usually while thinking about something else entirely.
That's close to half of daily life on something like autopilot.
So what exactly is a habit?
In everyday speech we use the word for anything we do often.
Researchers mean something narrower.
A habit is a behaviour that's triggered automatically by a situation, because you've done it in that situation many times before.
The key word is automatically.
You don't weigh it up.
The situation calls the action out of you, often before you've noticed.
That's different from a routine you choose each time.
If you go for a run because you've decided you want to be fitter, and you have to talk yourself into it every morning, that's a goal-driven behaviour.
It becomes a habit when putting on your running shoes after your morning coffee just happens, the way checking your mirrors happens when you change lanes.
Some of the clearest evidence for what's going on in the brain comes from the laboratory of Ann Graybiel at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology.
Her team recorded activity in a region deep in the brain called the basal ganglia while rats learned to run a simple T-shaped maze to find a food reward.
Early in training, the neurons were busy throughout the run, as the rat sniffed, hesitated and worked things out.
As the route became familiar, something striking happened.
The activity bunched up at the beginning and the end of the run, and went fairly quiet in the middle.
Researchers call this chunking.
The brain packages a sequence of actions into a single unit, marked by a clear start signal and a clear finish.
Once the chunk is triggered, it tends to run through to the end with little supervision.
Think of reversing out of your driveway.
Dozens of small movements, but you experience it as one smooth action, started by getting into the car.
This is why habits are so useful.
They free up attention for other things.
Imagine consciously deciding every movement involved in brushing your teeth.
But it's also why habits can be so stubborn.
A chunk that runs without supervision doesn't stop to ask whether it's still a good idea.
In the next part, we'll look at the ingredients that build a habit in the first place.
You've probably heard them described as cue, routine and reward.
That framework is broadly right, but the research adds some surprising twists.
Part two. Cues, routines and rewards.
The cue, routine and reward loop was made famous by the journalist Charles Duhigg in his 2012 book The Power of Habit.
It's a handy summary.
A cue triggers a routine, the routine brings a reward, and repeating that loop makes the link stronger.
Let's take each part in turn, starting with the one people most often overlook.
Cues can be almost anything that reliably comes just before the behaviour.
A place, like your kitchen bench.
A time of day.
Something you've just finished doing, like hanging up your keys.
Other people, like the colleague you always grab a coffee with.
Even a mood, like the restless boredom that sends your hand to your phone.
A lovely study from 2011 shows how powerful place cues are.
David Neal, Wendy Wood and their colleagues handed out popcorn to people as they went into a cinema.
Some got fresh popcorn.
Others got popcorn that had been popped a week earlier, and was stale, chewy and unpleasant.
People who rarely ate popcorn at the movies ate much less of the stale stuff, as you'd expect.
But people with a strong movie popcorn habit ate just about as much of the stale popcorn as the fresh.
They said they didn't like it.
They ate it anyway.
Then the researchers ran the same test in a different setting, a university meeting room where people watched music videos.
There, even the habitual popcorn eaters ate less of the stale popcorn.
Outside the cinema, their habit wasn't triggered, so their taste buds got a vote again.
The cue, not the craving, was running the show.
The routine is the behaviour itself, and the main thing to know is that simple routines become automatic faster than complicated ones.
Drinking a glass of water becomes a habit sooner than doing fifty sit-ups.
We'll come back to that shortly.
Then there's the reward.
When a behaviour produces something pleasant, the brain learns to repeat it.
Much of our understanding here comes from the neuroscientist Wolfram Schultz, who recorded the activity of dopamine neurons in monkeys receiving drops of juice.
He found that these neurons fired most strongly when a reward was better than expected.
Once the reward became perfectly predictable, the burst shifted earlier, to the cue that signalled the juice was coming.
That's an important twist.
Dopamine is often described as a pleasure chemical, but in this research it behaved more like a teaching signal.
It says, pay attention, this cue predicts something good.
That helps explain why an unpredictable reward, like a message that might or might not be waiting on your phone, can be so compelling.
The uncertainty keeps the teaching signal firing.
For building a habit, two practical lessons follow.
First, rewards work best when they're immediate.
The health benefits of exercise arrive in months, which is far too slow for the brain's habit machinery.
The good feeling of a hot shower afterwards, or a favourite podcast you only listen to on your walk, arrives right away.
Second, it helps if the behaviour itself becomes enjoyable, because then the reward is built in.
And here's the final twist, the one that surprises people most.
Once a habit is truly established, it can keep going even when the reward has gone.
Remember the stale popcorn.
Studies in both animals and people have shown the same pattern.
Early in learning, behaviour tracks the reward closely.
Once the behaviour becomes habitual, it becomes much less sensitive to whether the reward is still there.
That's exactly what makes good habits so durable.
It's also what makes bad ones so annoying.
Which brings us to the question almost everyone asks.
How long does all this take?
Part three. How long it really takes.
You've probably heard that it takes twenty-one days to form a habit.
It's one of the most repeated numbers in self-help.
It's also, as far as the research goes, not true.
The number seems to trace back to an American plastic surgeon called Maxwell Maltz.
In his bestselling 1960 book Psycho-Cybernetics, he observed that it seemed to take patients a minimum of about twenty-one days to get used to a change.
He was describing things like adjusting to a new face after surgery, or to the loss of a limb.
Notice the word minimum, and notice that he wasn't talking about forming habits at all.
Over the decades, a surgeon's rough observation got polished into a rule.
The first careful study of how long habits really take was led by the health psychologist Phillippa Lally at University College London, and published in 2010.
Ninety-six volunteers each chose a new healthy behaviour to do once a day in the same situation.
Some picked something simple, like drinking a bottle of water with lunch.
Others picked something harder, like running for fifteen minutes before dinner.
Every day for twelve weeks, they rated how automatic the behaviour felt.
They answered simple questions, such as whether they did it without having to consciously remember, and whether they'd find it hard not to do it.
For most people, automaticity rose quickly at first, then gradually levelled off, a bit like learning to drive.
The early repetitions made the biggest difference.
The average time to reach that levelling off was sixty-six days.
But the range was enormous, from eighteen days for some people to an estimated two hundred and fifty-four days for others.
And some people's behaviour never became automatic within the study at all.
Simpler behaviours tended to become habits faster than more demanding ones.
A larger picture arrived in 2024, when a team led by Ben Singh at the University of South Australia pulled together twenty studies involving more than two and a half thousand people.
The typical time to form a health habit, they found, was around two to five months.
The median sat at about two months, but individual times stretched from as little as four days to nearly a year.
That review turned up some interesting details.
In one of the studies it included, stretching done in the morning became habitual faster than stretching done in the evening.
Across the research, habits that people chose for themselves tended to form more strongly than ones assigned to them.
And a stable context, the same time and place each day, helped a great deal.
There's another finding from Lally's study that deserves to be much better known.
Missing one day didn't make any real difference to how the habit developed.
People who skipped an occasional day still got there.
This matters because many of us treat a single slip as proof that we've failed, and give up entirely.
The research says a missed day is a bump, not a reset.
What seems to matter is not letting one missed day turn into a missed fortnight.
So the honest answer to how long a habit takes is this.
Usually a couple of months.
Sometimes much longer.
It depends on the person, on how complicated the behaviour is, and on how consistently it's tied to the same cue.
If you're three weeks into a new habit and it still feels like effort, you're not doing it wrong.
You're right on schedule.
Those questions from Lally's study make a handy self-check, by the way.
You don't need a chart or an app.
Every so often, just ask yourself two things.
Did I do it today without having to remind myself?
And would it feel strange to skip it?
When the answer to both is a clear yes, the habit is doing the work for you, and you can stop relying on effort.
Now let's turn all of this into a practical toolkit, for building habits you want and loosening the ones you don't.
Part four. Building and breaking habits.
The first tool is the most thoroughly tested.
The psychologist Peter Gollwitzer called it an implementation intention, and it's simply a plan in the form, when this happens, I will do that.
Not, I'll exercise more.
But, when I get home from work on Monday, Wednesday and Friday, I'll put my walking shoes on before I sit down.
In a 2002 study in the United Kingdom, Sarah Milne, Sheina Orbell and Paschal Sheeran worked with a group of young adults.
They asked some of them to write down exactly when and where they would exercise over the next week.
Ninety-one per cent of that group exercised at least once.
In the comparison groups, which didn't make a specific plan, fewer than four in ten did.
A plan like that works because it builds the cue in advance.
You've decided what the trigger is, so your brain has something to attach the new behaviour to.
The second tool is related.
Link the new habit to one you already have.
The behaviour scientist B J Fogg at Stanford University popularised this in his work on tiny habits.
After I pour my morning coffee, I'll take my vitamins.
After I park the car at work, I'll check my calendar for the day.
Your existing habit becomes a ready-made, highly reliable cue.
The third tool is to start smaller than feels worthwhile.
Remember that simpler behaviours become automatic faster.
Two push-ups after brushing your teeth sounds almost silly.
But it's easy enough to do every day, and once the cue and action are firmly linked, it's easy to add more.
The fourth tool is friction, and it's one of Wendy Wood's favourite themes.
Small obstacles have a surprisingly large effect on what we do.
If your running gear is laid out by the bed, going for a run is easier.
If the biscuits are in a high cupboard behind the flour, snacking is harder.
Most of us put far too much faith in willpower, and far too little in rearranging the setting so the right choice is the easy one.
Interestingly, research suggests that people who seem to have great self-control often aren't resisting temptation more.
They're facing less of it, because they've built routines that keep them out of its way.
Self-control, in practice, often looks a lot like good habits.
Now for breaking a habit you don't want.
Because habits are triggered by cues, the most effective approach is usually to change or avoid the cue, rather than fighting the urge each time it arrives.
Charge your phone in the kitchen overnight rather than beside the bed.
Take a different route home if the old one goes past the drive-through.
Big life changes offer a special opportunity here.
In one study, Wendy Wood and her colleagues followed students who transferred to a new university.
For students whose old context changed, habits like exercising or watching television were disrupted, and they became more likely to act on their current intentions rather than their old routines.
Researchers sometimes call these moments habit discontinuities.
Moving house, starting a new job or going through another big change shakes up your cues, which makes it an unusually good time to start something new or leave something behind.
If you can't avoid the cue, try replacing the routine rather than simply deleting it.
If the three o'clock slump sends you to the vending machine, keep the cue and the break, but swap the routine for a short walk around the block.
You still get a reward, just a different one.
And just as with building habits, expect it to take a while, and don't let one slip become a surrender.
Let's put the whole toolkit together with an example.
Imagine someone called Mia who wants to start walking in the evenings, and wants to stop scrolling her phone in bed.
For the walk, she makes a plan.
When I get home and put my bag down, I'll change into my walking shoes.
She leaves the shoes right by the door, which removes friction.
She starts with just ten minutes around the block, and saves a favourite podcast for the walk only, so there's an immediate reward.
For the scrolling, she doesn't rely on willpower at bedtime.
She changes the cue, and charges her phone in the kitchen, with a cheap alarm clock beside the bed instead.
Some nights she'll slip.
That's fine.
In a couple of months, if she keeps at it, the evening walk will probably feel as natural as locking the front door.
If you'd like one small thing to try on your next walk or drive, pick a habit you want.
Then say to yourself, out loud if you like, when this happens, I will do that.
Choose a cue you already meet every day.
That single sentence is the most reliable habit tool researchers have found.
To sum up, habits are behaviours that situations trigger automatically, and cues matter far more than we tend to think.
They usually take around two to five months to form rather than twenty-one days, and missing a single day doesn't reset the clock.
To build one, tie it to a clear cue, start small and reduce the friction.
To break one, change the cue rather than relying on willpower.
Quick recall. Answer out loud, or just in your head.
Question one. In Phillippa Lally's 2010 study, what was the average time for a new behaviour to become automatic?
Answer. Sixty-six days, with a very wide range.
Question two. In the stale popcorn study, why did habitual popcorn eaters keep eating the stale popcorn in the cinema?
Answer. The cinema setting triggered the habit, whether or not they liked the popcorn.
Question three. What is an implementation intention?
Answer. A plan in the form, when this happens, I will do that.
That's the end of How Habits Actually Form. See you on the next one.
